bearings.paper_claim: Per-candidate PAC limits bind for 14.4 percent of candidates receiving any PAC money (text Section 3, p.8; not in Table 1). Firm-cycles at the limit show +549,166 dollars of lobbying per cycle (Table 3 col 1, SE 225,013; 2000-2008, 787 firms, 2,783 firm-cycles, pooled across the 2002 BCRA break). Firms at the limit show CEO giving 0.066 more likely (Table 2, 1992-2008, 950 firms). Authors say PAC limits are effectively non-binding and all estimates are partial correlations.
bearings.paper_location: Section 3 p.8; Table 2 p.28; Table 3 p.29; Section 1 pp.3-5; Conclusion p.19
bearings.system_side: The optimizer caps each member at PMAX = 10,000 dollars above existing CU money, read as one CU PAC per-candidate per-cycle limit (Paul 2026-09-30 ruling, quoted in the code comment). Nothing outside the PAC channel is modeled.
bearings.code_ref: fec/engine/optimize.py:23-27 (PMAX and pot comment); fec/engine/optimize.py:71 (marg cap check)
bearings.transfer_conditions: Cap mechanics transfer if the 10,000 per-cycle limit is the same. The paper does not say the limit is unindexed; that is an assumption not stated in the paper. Spillover magnitudes come from large S&P 500 for-profit firms, not CU PACs, and are partial correlations. Supports a caveat that PMAX bounds PAC dollars only; does not justify reweighting.
bearings.verifier_note: Code and table values verified. Fixes: the 14.4 percent figure is in the text at p.8, not Table 1; the paper says PAC limits are non-binding, not total corporate political activity; the 549,166 figure pools the BCRA break and needs an UNSTRATIFIED label; the unindexed claim is not in the paper.

bearings.paper_claim: Firm-cycles whose PAC reaches the limit are associated with 549,000 to 1.6M dollars more lobbying per cycle (abstract; Table 3 col 1; Table 5) and with about 110 dollars more CEO giving per candidate at the limit (Table 2). CEO giving is candidate money outside the PAC channel. Authors describe these as partial correlations.
bearings.paper_location: Abstract p.1; Table 2 p.28; Table 3 p.29; Table 5 p.30
bearings.system_side: The b leg of pflip counts competitor money as bank plus finserv PAC dollars per member (ind0), loaded from data/engine/congestion.json, with median imputation for unobserved members. Executive giving and competitor lobbying are not in ind0.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Hypothesis only: if competitor bank and finserv firms hit the cap as S&P 500 PAC firms do, ind0 undercounts competitor pressure on the members they max out. The paper does not test this. Does not license LDA dollars as a per-member weight (D-021).
bearings.verifier_note: Code references and median imputation verified. The paper reports co-occurrence with the limit, not that firms move resources, so reword as associated. The undercount is an inference, not a finding.

bearings.paper_claim: Within firm-cycle and candidate-cycle fixed effects, a candidate receiving the PAC maximum is 0.066 more likely (SE 0.006) to receive a CEO gift and receives about 110 dollars more (SE 10.05) (Table 2; 1992-2008; 950 firms; 6,803,661 observations). The text reports 7.7 percent and 123 dollars, which do not match Table 2. Table 7 gives 123.88.

The paper does not say whether P(joined given lobbied) is 1 by construction; the REFUTED-as-influence verdict comes from the analyst and the brain, not this code or the paper.

summary_issues: The 549,000 lobbying figure and the 1.6M to 3.0M RD range are pooled across the 2002 BCRA break (2000-2008; one pre-BCRA lobbying cycle). Under the stratification rule they need an UNSTRATIFIED label or stratified figures; the summary states them without one.

The summary says the CEO effect is about 110 dollars more on average. Table 2 is the dollar effect for a candidate at the PAC maximum, conditional on firm-cycle and candidate-cycle fixed effects, not an average across candidates.

Summary figures lack windows and denominators: the 6.6-point CEO effect (1992-2008, 950 firms), the 549,000 lobbying effect (2000-2008, 787 firms, 2,783 firm-cycles), and the 14.4 percent at-limit share (text p.8, of recipients). Only the flags carry them.

The summary and bearing 1 say limits are non-binding on total corporate political activity. The paper says corporate PAC limits are effectively non-binding and that spillovers can be economically meaningful.
Bearing text uses causal verbs (move, spend more) for estimates the authors call partial correlations. The summary's flags say partial correlation; the bearings should match.
The summary's claim that the limit is unindexed is not in the paper and is unverified.
The paul_alignment claim that Paul's component notes expect donations to lead lobbying cannot be checked: the item has no paul_entries and no annotations (n_annots 0). Treat as unverified.

The related-link rationales were checked only for existence and title (all nine slugs are real items); their content claims were not re-read. Table 3 columns 4-5 at-limit values do not print in the extraction; only columns 1, 2, 3 and 6 are verified.
